nodes.label: Circular measure: degrees, minutes and seconds
nodes.description: Use the degree as the circular measuring unit (1° = 60', 1' = 60''); convert between D° M' S'' form and decimal degrees, by hand and with the calculator.

nodes.label: The main trigonometric ratios of an acute angle
nodes.description: In a right-angled triangle, identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse for an acute angle; define sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent.

nodes.label: Computing trigonometric ratios in right triangles
nodes.description: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side, then compute the ratios of the two acute angles; verify identities such as sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

nodes.label: Exact trigonometric ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°
nodes.description: Derive the exact ratios from the half-equilateral triangle (sides 1 : 2 : √3) and the isosceles right triangle (sides 1 : 1 : √2); recall the table of exact values.

nodes.label: Evaluating expressions with special angles
nodes.description: Evaluate numeric expressions in sin, cos and tan of 30°, 45°, 60°; use sin θ = cos (90° − θ) and tan θ = sin θ / cos θ.

nodes.label: Finding the acute angle given its trigonometric ratio
nodes.description: Recover the angle from an exact special-angle ratio or with the calculator inverse keys, expressing answers in degrees, minutes and seconds.

nodes.label: Trigonometry in geometric applications
nodes.description: Apply trigonometric ratios inside geometric figures (isosceles and equilateral triangles): drop a perpendicular, then find angles, sides and areas.

questions.stem: One degree is divided into…
solution: The degree is the circular measuring unit, and its parts are: $1^\circ = 60'$ (minutes) and $1' = 60''$ (seconds).
So one degree is divided into 60 minutes.
questions.source_note: Original question; parts of a degree, Lesson 4-1, p.49

questions.stem: Express $30'$ (thirty minutes) as a part of a degree, in decimal form.
solution: Since $1^\circ = 60'$, divide the minutes by 60 to convert to degrees.
questions.source_note: Original question; minute-to-degree conversion, Lesson 4-1, p.50

questions.stem: Write $45^\circ\ 30'$ in degrees as a decimal number.
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Drill 1, Lesson 4-1, p.50

questions.stem: $20.25^\circ$ written in degrees and minutes equals…
solution: The whole part stays as degrees: $20^\circ$.
Convert the decimal part to minutes: $0.25^\circ = 0.25 \times 60 = 15'$.
So $20.25^\circ = 20^\circ\ 15'$ — note $0.25^\circ$ is NOT $25'$, because a degree has 60 minutes, not 100.
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Drill 2, Lesson 4-1, p.50

questions.stem: Write $62^\circ\ 45'\ 36''$ in degrees as a decimal number.
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Drill 1 (D° M' S'' to decimal), Lesson 4-1, p.50

questions.stem: $28.51^\circ$ written in degrees, minutes and seconds equals…
solution: Convert the decimal part to minutes: $0.51^\circ = 0.51 \times 60 = 30.6'$.
Keep $30'$ and convert the remaining $0.6'$ to seconds: $0.6' = 0.6 \times 60 = 36''$.
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Drill 2 (decimal to D° M' S''), Lesson 4-1, p.50

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$ right-angled at $B$: $\sin C =$ …
solution: For the acute angle $C$: the side opposite is $AB$, the side adjacent is $BC$, and the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle) is $AC$.
Careful: $\frac{BC}{AC}$ is $\cos C$ (adjacent over hypotenuse), not $\sin C$.
questions.source_note: Original question; definition of sine, Lesson 4-1, p.50–51

questions.stem: For an acute angle in a right-angled triangle, the tangent of the angle equals…
solution: So the tangent is opposite ÷ adjacent — swapping them (adjacent ÷ opposite) is the classic mistake.
questions.source_note: Original question; definition of tangent, Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$, with $AB = 3$ cm, $BC = 4$ cm and $AC = 5$ cm. Then $\cos C =$ …
solution: For angle $C$: adjacent side $= BC = 4$, hypotenuse $= AC = 5$.
($\frac{3}{5}$ is $\sin C$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ is $\tan C$ — don't mix opposite with adjacent.)
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Example 1, Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $XYZ$ is a triangle right-angled at $Y$, with $XY = 6$ cm, $YZ = 8$ cm and $XZ = 10$ cm. Then $\tan Z =$ …
solution: For angle $Z$: opposite side $= XY = 6$, adjacent side $= YZ = 8$.
($\frac{4}{3}$ comes from swapping opposite and adjacent — that would be $\tan X$, not $\tan Z$.)
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Example 1, Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$. If $\sin C = 0.6$ and $AC = 15$ cm, find the length of $AB$ in cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; applying the sine definition, Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$, so $A$ and $C$ are two complementary acute angles. Then $\sin A =$ …
solution: For angle $A$: the opposite side is $BC$, so $\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}$.
For angle $C$: the adjacent side is also $BC$, so $\cos C = \frac{BC}{AC}$.
The two ratios use the same sides, so $\sin A = \cos C$: the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complementary angle.
questions.source_note: Original question; extends Example 1B (ratios of both acute angles), Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $C$, with $AC = 3$ cm and $BC = 4$ cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse $AB$ in cm.
solution: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, so it is $AB$.
questions.source_note: Original question; Pythagoras step of Example 1A, Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: For any acute angle $C$ in a right-angled triangle: $\sin^2 C + \cos^2 C =$ …
solution: Write the ratios with sides: $\sin C = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$ and $\cos C = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$.
By the Pythagorean theorem $\text{opp}^2 + \text{adj}^2 = \text{hyp}^2$, so the ratio equals $1$.
questions.source_note: Original question; identity proved in Drill (sin²C + cos²C = 1), Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $C$, with $AB = 10$ cm and $BC = 8$ cm. Find $\sin B$ as a decimal.
solution: First find the missing side: $(AC)^2 = (AB)^2 - (BC)^2 = 100 - 64 = 36$, so $AC = 6$ cm.
For angle $B$: opposite side $= AC = 6$, hypotenuse $= AB = 10$.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Example 1 (find side, then ratio), Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $C$, with $AB = 25$ cm and $AC = 7$ cm. Then $\tan A =$ …
solution: Find the missing side: $(BC)^2 = (AB)^2 - (AC)^2 = 625 - 49 = 576$, so $BC = 24$ cm.
For angle $A$: opposite side $= BC = 24$, adjacent side $= AC = 7$.
$\tan A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{24}{7}$. ($\frac{7}{24}$ is $\tan B$ — the opposite/adjacent swap.)
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Example 1, Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: If $\theta$ is an acute angle and $\sin \theta = \frac{5}{13}$, then $\cos \theta =$ …
solution: Take a right triangle where the side opposite $\theta$ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13.
questions.source_note: Original question; ratios of the 5-12-13 triangle (cf. 5-12-13 in Example 1), Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: If $\tan A = \frac{3}{4}$ where $A$ is an acute angle, find the value of $25 \sin A \cos A$.
solution: $\tan A = \frac{3}{4}$ means opposite $= 3$ and adjacent $= 4$ in a right triangle; the hypotenuse $= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$.
questions.source_note: Original question; extends Example 1C style (products of ratios), Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: $\sin 30^\circ =$ …
solution: In the half-equilateral triangle the sides are in ratio $1 : 2 : \sqrt{3}$, and the side opposite $30^\circ$ is the shortest one.
questions.source_note: Original question; special-angle table, Lesson 4-2, p.52–53

questions.stem: $\tan 45^\circ =$ …
solution: In the isosceles right triangle the two legs are equal ($1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$).
questions.source_note: Original question; 45° ratios from the isosceles right triangle, Lesson 4-2, p.53

questions.stem: $\cos 60^\circ =$ …
solution: In the half-equilateral triangle, the side adjacent to the $60^\circ$ angle is the shortest side (ratio 1) and the hypotenuse is 2.
questions.source_note: Original question; 30°/60° ratios from the equilateral triangle, Lesson 4-2, p.52

questions.stem: $\tan 30^\circ =$ …
solution: In the half-equilateral triangle: side opposite $30^\circ$ is 1, side adjacent to $30^\circ$ is $\sqrt{3}$.
questions.source_note: Original question; special-angle table, Lesson 4-2, p.52–53

questions.stem: Find the value of: $2 \sin 30^\circ + \tan 45^\circ$.
questions.source_note: Original question; first use of the table values, Lesson 4-2, p.53

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$, with $m(\angle C) = 30^\circ$ and $AC = 8$ cm. Find the length of $AB$ in cm.
solution: $AB$ is the side opposite angle $C$, and $AC$ is the hypotenuse.
questions.source_note: Original question; applying sin 30° = 1/2 in a triangle, Lesson 4-2, p.52–53

questions.stem: $\sin 30^\circ = \cos \dots^\circ$
solution: The sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complementary angle (the two angles add up to $90^\circ$).
questions.source_note: Original question; Remark 1 and Drill (sin 30° = cos …°), Lesson 4-2, p.52–53

questions.stem: For any acute angle $A$: $\tan A =$ …
questions.source_note: Original question; Remark 2 (tan A = sin A / cos A), Lesson 4-2, p.53

questions.stem: Find the value of: $\sin 60^\circ \cos 30^\circ - \sin 30^\circ$ (as a decimal).
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Example 1, Lesson 4-2, p.54

questions.stem: Find the value of: $\tan^2 60^\circ + \tan^2 45^\circ$.
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Example 1 and Drill (squares of ratios), Lesson 4-2, p.54

questions.stem: Find the value of: $\left(\cos^2 45^\circ + \sin^2 30^\circ\right) \div \tan^2 30^\circ$ (as a decimal).
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Example 1B (compound expression), Lesson 4-2, p.54

questions.stem: The value of $\dfrac{\sin 60^\circ \tan 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ}{\cos^2 30^\circ}$ is…
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Example 1B, Lesson 4-2, p.54

questions.stem: If $\sin X = \frac{1}{2}$ where $X$ is an acute angle, then $m(\angle X) =$ …
solution: From the special-angle table, the acute angle whose sine is $\frac{1}{2}$ is $30^\circ$.
So $m(\angle X) = 30^\circ$. (It is $\cos 60^\circ$ that equals $\frac{1}{2}$, not $\sin 60^\circ$.)
questions.source_note: Original question; scope of Drill 1 (sin X = 1/2), Lesson 4-2, p.56

questions.stem: If $\tan X = 1$ where $X$ is an acute angle, then $m(\angle X) =$ …
solution: $\tan 45^\circ = 1$ (the two legs of the isosceles right triangle are equal).
questions.source_note: Original question; angle from an exact ratio, Lesson 4-2, p.55–56

questions.stem: If $\cos X = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ where $X$ is an acute angle, find $m(\angle X)$ in degrees.
questions.source_note: Original question; angle from an exact ratio, Lesson 4-2, p.55–56

questions.stem: If $\tan (X + 15^\circ) = \sqrt{3}$ where $X$ is an acute angle, find $m(\angle X)$ in degrees.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Drill 4 (tan (X+10) = √3), Lesson 4-2, p.56

questions.stem: If $\tan 3X = \sqrt{3}$ where $3X$ is an acute angle, find $m(\angle X)$ in degrees.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Drill 5 (tan 2X = √3), Lesson 4-2, p.56

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ where $D \in \overline{BC}$. Then $\cos B =$ …
solution: In an isosceles triangle, the perpendicular from the vertex bisects the base, so $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ and $BD = 6$ cm.
Triangle $ABD$ is right-angled at $D$: for angle $B$, adjacent $= BD = 6$ and hypotenuse $= AB = 10$.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as the 10-10-12 Drill, Lesson 4-1 p.51 / Example 4, Lesson 4-2, p.55–56

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ where $D \in \overline{BC}$. Find $\sin B$ as a decimal.
solution: $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$, so $BD = 6$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Example 4 (perpendicular to the base), Lesson 4-2, p.55–56

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. Find the area of the triangle in cm².
solution: Draw $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$; then $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ and $BD = 6$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Example 4 second part (area via the height), Lesson 4-2, p.55–56

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ where $D \in \overline{BC}$. Find $\tan (\angle CAD)$ as a decimal.
solution: $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$, so $CD = 6$ cm, and $AD = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8$ cm.
In right triangle $ACD$ (right-angled at $D$): for angle $CAD$, opposite $= CD = 6$ and adjacent $= AD = 8$.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as the Drill (sin/cos/tan of ∠CAD), Lesson 4-1, p.51

questions.stem: The height of an equilateral triangle whose side length is $6$ cm equals…
solution: The height from a vertex makes a right triangle in which the side of the triangle is the hypotenuse and the base angle is $60^\circ$.
questions.source_note: Original question; equilateral-triangle setup of Think and Discuss, Lesson 4-2, p.52

visuals.caption: One degree cut into 60 minutes — watch where a quarter, a half and three quarters of a degree land.
An angle is measured in degrees, minutes and seconds — this one opens up to 36° 52' 12''.

visuals.question: q:u4-1-2:001
visuals.caption: Sine is the opposite side over the hypotenuse — watch the two sides light up.

visuals.question: q:u4-1-2:003
visuals.caption: Cosine is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse — the side touching the angle, not the one facing it.

visuals.question: q:u4-1-2:002
visuals.caption: Tangent is opposite over adjacent — no hypotenuse involved.

visuals.question: q:u4-1-3:005
visuals.caption: Given one ratio, Pythagoras hands you the missing side — then every other ratio follows.

visuals.question: q:u4-1-3:003
visuals.caption: Build the triangle side by side: legs 6 and 8, and Pythagoras makes the hypotenuse 10.
Half an equilateral triangle: sides 1, √3 and 2 — that is where sin 30° = 1/2 comes from.

visuals.question: q:u4-2-1:002
visuals.caption: The isosceles right triangle: two equal legs, so tan 45° = 1.

visuals.question: q:u4-2-1:003
visuals.caption: Same half-equilateral triangle seen from the 60° corner: cos 60° = 1/2.
Sine climbs as the acute angle grows — compare 30°, 45° and 60°.

visuals.question: q:u4-2-2:001
visuals.caption: Sine of an angle = cosine of its complement — the pairs always add up to 90°.

visuals.question: q:u4-2-3:001
visuals.caption: Opposite 1, hypotenuse 2 — which acute angle has sine 1/2?
The three special angles sit between 0° and 90° — going backwards from a ratio lands you on one of them.

visuals.question: q:u4-2-4:002
visuals.caption: Drop the height of the isosceles triangle and two equal right triangles appear — trigonometry can start.

visuals.question: q:u4-2-4:001
visuals.caption: Inside the half-triangle: adjacent 6, hypotenuse 10, so cos B = 3/5.
